title: New Orleans musicians homesick in New York
summary: Most New Orleans musicians pined for home; Kmen recalls spot jobs with Bill Bourgeois.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: What about George Horton? Was he playing trumpet there? He played trumpet.

He also played bass, but primarily trumpet. And in fact he played some darn good trumpet as I remember. Some really good New Orleans trumpet. But it was a hard thing to get into. Johnny Beresdorf was up there playing good trumpet too. But one thing I noticed about most of the New Orleans guys, with very few exceptions, they were pining for New Orleans all the time. Longing to get back and it didn't take much to convince them that they belonged back to New Orleans. That's a trait peculiar to the city. The people that are born here seem to find it very hard to live happily anywhere else.
Well, there's something unique about the town. It's got to be.
Whether it's the coffee or the Mardi Gras or something.
Well, Pete Fountain, when they gave this Welcome Back Pete concert over at Macalice, he said it was French bread that he longed all night in.
And others talking about red beans and rye. Right. But I know you worked some dates with Bill Bourgeois.

Yes, I did with George Hartman too. We'd pick up spot jobs here and there. In fact, when I came to this town after all those many years, Bill Bourgeois reminded me that we had played together for a Jewish leader up in New York at a dance celebrating Hitler's birthday. His memory was better than mine though. I'd forgotten it until he mentioned it. And you know, you had a clique and you tried to help each other out with spot jobs. So we'd actually moved around somewhat and meet them off and together on jobs.
